newsitem.title: UK: Royal Bank buys Midshires building society.
newsitem.headline: Royal Bank buys Midshires building society.

text.p: Royal Bank of Scotland said on Wednesday it would buy Britain's Birmingham Midshires, giving the building society's members an average 600 pound ($947) handout.
But Royal Bank stressed the 605 million pound plus purchase of Birmingham Midshires, the fifth largest of Britain's traditional home loan providers did not fulfil its ambitions.

"We do not regard this as a deal which transforms the Royal Bank group. And we would be interested, if the right deal comes along, in the deal that would (transform the group)," Royal Bank chief executive George Mathewson told a telephone news briefing.
"In no way does this mean we would not be interested in a very much larger transaction."
Royal Bank's shares had fallen 19 pence to 606.5 pence by 1115 GMT, after earlier rising four pence on news of the deal.
Royal Bank will pay between 605 and 630 million pounds for Birmingham Midshires. The middle of this range implies a price/earnings ratio of 12 times normalised earnings, it said.

Birmingham Midshire's chief executive Mike Jackson, who will be offered a place on the Royal Bank board when the deal is completed in the second half of 1998, said the mutually-owned society's members would be "delighted".

"This is a good deal for our members, staff and customers," Jackson told Reuters in an interview. Job losses will be limited to around 300 as a result of the closure of a mortgage processing centre at Bracknell, in the south of England.
By closing the centre, Birmingham Midshires will save around eight million pounds.
Banking union BIFU gave the takeover a cautious welcome, applauding an undertaking to maintain jobs, services and Birmingham Midshires' 115 branches for at least three years.
Birmingham Midshires Building Society has a 150-year-old mutual tradition. It is owned by its savers and borrowers. Around a million will qualify for Royal Bank of Scotland preference shares or cash.
Birmingham Midshires is following a route taken earlier this year by another building society Bristol and West, which was bought by Bank of Ireland for 600 million pounds.
Jackson said the decision had been taken after a two-year review of the society's options, adding it had been approached by Royal Bank nine months ago.
This approach had come at roughly the same time the society had decided it was interested in a partnership with the Edinburgh-based bank, he added.

Royal Bank's Mathewson dismissed concerns about Birmingham Midshires' relatively high cost income ratio, stressing he was confident the level could be brought down to "competitive levels" by a combination of cost cutting and increasing volumes.
The deal is expected to have a neutral effect on Royal Bank's earnings per share in the first year and to be earnings enhancing after this.
Mathewson said Royal Bank did not anticipate any regulatory hurdles derailing the deal, which will bring its mortgage book up to 13 billion pounds, over three percent over the British market.

Royal Bank's corporate business has been growing strongly and there was a need to balance this by increasing its retail assets. This strategy was already being pursued via its Direct Line insurance arm and in a joint venture with supermarket group Tesco Plc, he added.
But the deal was not good news for Sun Life & Provincial Holdings Plc, which will see an appointed representative agreement with Birmingham Midshires disappear in a year's time.

After announcing the deal, Royal Bank said it had agreed to place 33.4 million new shares with Scottish Widows' Fund and Life Assurances Society at a price of 601 pence a share. As a result Scottish Widows will hold a 4.96 percent stake in the bank.
Royal Bank said the placing would be used to supplement its capital resources, adding it would fund the Birmingham Midshires buy without recourse to an equity issue.
